AS-14.2.17.text: The powder of khadyota (fire-fly) mixed with the oil of mustard seeds emits light at night.
AS-14.2.17.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 17 (AS-14.2.17)

AS-14.2.18.text: The powder of khadyota (fire-fly) and gandúpada (earth-worm) or the powder of ocean animals mixed with the powder of bhringa (malabathrum), kapála (a pot-herb), and khadira (mimosa catechu), and karnikára (pentapetes acerifolia), combined with the oil of sakuna (a bird) and kanka (vulture), is tejanachúrna (ignition powder).
AS-14.2.18.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 18 (AS-14.2.18)

AS-14.2.19.text: When the body of a man is rubbed over with the powder of the charcoal of the bark of páribhadraka (erythrina indica) mixed with the serum of the flesh of mandúka (a frog), it can be burnt with fire (without causing hurt).
AS-14.2.19.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 19 (AS-14.2.19)

AS-14.2.2.text: The powder of másha (phraseolus radiatus), yava (barley), kuluttha (horse-gram) and the root of darbha (sacrificial grass) mixed with milk and clarified butter; the milk of valli (a kind of creeper) and clarified butter derived from it and mixed in equal proportions and combined with the paste prepared from the root of sála (shorea robusta) and prisniparni (hedysarum lagopodioides), when drunk with milk; or a dose of milk mixed with clarified butter and spirituous liquor, both prepared from the above substances, enables one to fast for a month.
AS-14.2.2.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 2 (AS-14.2.2)

AS-14.2.20.text: The body which is painted with the pastry (kalka) prepared from the bark of páribhadraka (erythrina indica) and sesamum seeds burns with fire.
AS-14.2.20.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 20 (AS-14.2.20)

AS-14.2.21.text: The ball prepared from the powder of the charcoal of the bark of pílu (careya arborea) can be held in hand and burnt with fire.
AS-14.2.21.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 21 (AS-14.2.21)

AS-14.2.22.text: When the body of a man is smeared over with the serum of the flesh of a frog, it burns with fire (with no hurt).
AS-14.2.22.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 22 (AS-14.2.22)

AS-14.2.23.text: When the body of a man is smeared over with the above serum as well as with the oil extracted from the fruits of kusa (ficus religiosa), and ámra (mango tree), and when the powder prepared from an ocean frog (samdura mandúki), phenaka (sea-foam), and sarjarasa (the juice of vatica robusta) is sprinkled over the body, it burns with fire (without being hurt).
AS-14.2.23.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 23 (AS-14.2.23)

AS-14.2.24.text: When the body of a man is smeared over with sesamum oil mixed with equal quantities of the serum of the flesh of a frog, crab, and other animals, it can burn with fire (without hurt).
AS-14.2.24.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 24 (AS-14.2.24)

AS-14.2.25.text: The body which is smeared over with the serum of the flesh of a frog burns with fire.
AS-14.2.25.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 25 (AS-14.2.25)

AS-14.2.26.text: The body of a man, which is rubbed over with the powder of the root of bamboo (venu) and saivála (aquatic plant), and is smeared over with the serum of the flesh of a frog, burns with fire.
AS-14.2.26.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 26 (AS-14.2.26)

AS-14.2.27.text: Whoever has anointed his legs with the oil extracted from the paste prepared from the roots of páribhadraka (erythrina indica), pratibala (?), vanjula (a kind of ratan or tree), vajra (andropogon muricatum or euphorbia), and kadali (banana), mixed with the serum of the flesh of a frog, can walk over fire (without hurt).
AS-14.2.27.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 27 (AS-14.2.27)

AS-14.2.28.text: Oil should be extracted from the paste prepared from the roots of pratibala, vanjula and páribhadraka, all growing near water, the paste being mixed with the serum of the flesh of a frog.
AS-14.2.28.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 28 (AS-14.2.28)

AS-14.2.29.text: Having anointed one's legs with this oil, one can walk over a white-hot mass of fire as though on a bed of roses.
AS-14.2.29.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 29 (AS-14.2.29)

AS-14.2.3.text: The oil prepared from mustard seeds previously kept for seven nights in the urine of a white goat will, when used (externally) after keeping the oil inside a large bitter gourd for a month and a half, alter the colour of both biped and quadruped animals.
AS-14.2.3.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 3 (AS-14.2.3)

AS-14.2.30.text: When birds such as a hamsa (goose), krauncha (heron), mayúra (peacock) and other large swimming birds are let to fly at night with a burning reed attached to their tail it presents the appearance of a fire-brand falling from the sky (ulká).
AS-14.2.30.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 30 (AS-14.2.30)

AS-14.2.31.text: When, in a fireplace, kidney beans (másha) wetted with the menstrual fluid of a woman, as well as the roots of vajra (andropogon muricatum) and kadali (banana), wetted with the serum of the flesh of a frog are kept, no grains can be cooked there.
AS-14.2.31.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 31 (AS-14.2.31)

AS-14.2.32.text: By keeping in the mouth a ball-like piece of pilu (careya arberea) or a knot of the root of linseed tree (suvarchala) with fire inserted within the mass of the ball and wound round with threads and cotton (pichu), volumes of smoke and fire can be breathed out.
AS-14.2.32.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 32 (AS-14.2.32)

AS-14.2.33.text: When the oil extracted from the fruits of kusa (ficus religiosa) and ámra (mango) is poured over the fire, it burns even in the storm.
AS-14.2.33.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 33 (AS-14.2.33)

AS-14.2.34.text: Sea-foam wetted with oil and ignited keeps burning when floating on water.
AS-14.2.34.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 34 (AS-14.2.34)

AS-14.2.35.text: The fire generated by churning the bone of a monkey by means of a bamboo stick of white and black colour (kalmáshavenu) burns in water instead of being quenched.
AS-14.2.35.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 35 (AS-14.2.35)

AS-14.2.36.text: There will burn no other fire where the fire generated by churning, by means of a bamboo stick of white and black colour, the left side rib-bone of a man killed by a weapon or put to the gallows; or the fire generated by churning the bone of a man or woman by means of the bone of another man is circumambulated thrice from right to left.
AS-14.2.36.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 36 (AS-14.2.36)

AS-14.2.37.text: When the paste prepared from the animals such as chuchundari (musk-rat), khanjaríta (?) and khárakíta (?), with the urine of a horse is applied to the chains with which the legs of a man are bound, they will be broken to pieces.
AS-14.2.37.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 37 (AS-14.2.37)

AS-14.2.38.text: The sun-stone (ayaskánta) or any other stone (will break to pieces) when wetted with the serum of the flesh of the animals kulinda (?), dardura (?), and khárakíta (?).
AS-14.2.38.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 38 (AS-14.2.38)

AS-14.2.39.text: The paste prepared from the powder of the rib-bone of náraka (?), a donkey, kanka (a kind of vulture), and bhása (a bird), mixed with the juice of water-lily, is applied to the legs of bipeds and quadrupeds (while making a journey).
AS-14.2.39.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 39 (AS-14.2.39)

AS-14.2.4.text: The oil extracted from white mustard seeds mixed with the barley-corns contained in the dung of a white donkey, which has been living for more than seven nights on a diet of butter, milk and barley, causes alteration in colour.
AS-14.2.4.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 4 (AS-14.2.4)

AS-14.2.40.text: When a man makes a journey, wearing the shoes made of the skin of a camel, smeared over with the serum of the flesh of an owl and a vulture and covered over with the leaves of the banyan tree, he can walk fifty yojanas without any fatigue.
AS-14.2.40.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 40 (AS-14.2.40)

AS-14.2.41.text: (When the shoes are smeared over with) the pith, marrow or sperm of the birds, syena, kanka, káka, gridhra, hamsá, krauncha, and vichiralla, (the traveller wearing them) can walk a hundred yojanas (without any fatigue).
AS-14.2.41.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 41 (AS-14.2.41)

AS-14.2.42.text: The fat or serum derived from roasting a pregnant camel together with saptaparna (lechites scholaris) or from roasting dead children in cremation grounds, is applied to render a journey of a hundred yojanas easy.
AS-14.2.42.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 42 (AS-14.2.42)

AS-14.2.43.text: Terror should be caused to the enemy by exhibiting these and other wonderful and delusive performances; while anger causing terror is common to all, terrification by such wonders is held as a means to consolidate peace.
AS-14.2.43.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 43 (AS-14.2.43)

AS-14.2.5.text: The oil prepared from mustard seeds which have been previously kept in the urine and fluid dung of any of the two animals, a white goat and a white donkey, causes (when applied) such white colour as that of the fibre of arka plant or the down of a (white) bird.
AS-14.2.5.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 5 (AS-14.2.5)

AS-14.2.6.text: The mixture of the dung of a white cock and ajagara (boa-constrictor) causes white colour.
AS-14.2.6.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 6 (AS-14.2.6)

AS-14.2.7.text: The pastry made from white mustard seeds kept for seven nights in the urine of a white goat mixed with butter-milk, the milk of arka plant, salt, and grains (dhánya), causes, when applied for a fortnight, white colour.
AS-14.2.7.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 7 (AS-14.2.7)

AS-14.2.8.text: The paste, prepared from white mustard seeds which have been previously kept within a large bitter gourd and with clarified butter prepared from the milk of valli (a creeper) for half a month, makes the hair white.
AS-14.2.8.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 8 (AS-14.2.8)

AS-14.2.9.text: A bitter gourd, a stinking insect (pútikíta), and a white house-lizard; when a paste prepared from these is applied to the hair, the latter becomes as white as a conch-shell.
AS-14.2.9.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 2, Sutra 9 (AS-14.2.9)

AS-14.3.1.text: HAVING pulled out both the right and the left eye-balls of a cat, camel, wolf, boar, porcupine, váguli (?), naptri (?), crow and owl, or of any one, two, or three, or many of such animals as roam at nights, one should reduce them to two kinds of powder. Whoever anoints his own right eye with the powder of the left eye and his left eye with the powder of the right eye-ball can clearly see things even in pitch dark at night.
AS-14.3.1.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 1 (AS-14.3.1)

AS-14.3.10.text: Such are the eight kinds of the contrivances causing invisibility.
AS-14.3.10.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 10 (AS-14.3.10)

AS-14.3.11.text: I bow to Bali, son of Virochana; to Sambara acquainted with a hundred kinds of magic; to Bhandírapáka, Naraka, Nikumbha, and Kumbha.
AS-14.3.11.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 11 (AS-14.3.11)

AS-14.3.12.text: I bow to Devala and Nárada; I bow to Sávarnigálava; with the permission of these I cause deep slumber to thee.
AS-14.3.12.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 12 (AS-14.3.12)

AS-14.3.13.text: Just as the snakes, known as ajagara (boa-constrictor) fall into deep slumber, so may the rogues of the army who are very anxious to keep watch over the village;
AS-14.3.13.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 13 (AS-14.3.13)

AS-14.3.14.text: With their thousands of dogs (bhandaka) and hundreds of ruddy geese and donkeys, fall into deep slumber; I shall enter this house, and may the dogs be quiet.
AS-14.3.14.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 14 (AS-14.3.14)

AS-14.3.15.text: Having bowed to Manu, and having tethered the roguish dogs (sunakaphelaka), and having also bowed to those gods who are in heaven, and to Bráhmans among mankind;
AS-14.3.15.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 15 (AS-14.3.15)

AS-14.3.16.text: To those who are well versed in their Vedic studies, those who have attained to Kailása (a mountain of god Siva) by observing penance, and to all prophets, I do cause deep slumber to thee.
AS-14.3.16.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 16 (AS-14.3.16)

AS-14.3.17.text: The fan (chamari) comes out; may all combinations retire. Oblation to Manu, O Aliti and Paliti.
AS-14.3.17.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 17 (AS-14.3.17)

AS-14.3.18.text: Having fasted for three nights, one should, on the fourteenth day of the dark half of the month, the day being assigned to the star of Pushya, purchase from a low-caste woman (svapáki) vilikhávalekhana (finger nails?). Having kept them in a basket (kandolika), one should bury them apart in cremation grounds. Having unearthed them on the next fourteenth day, one should reduce them to a paste with kumári (aloe ?) and prepare small pills out of the paste. Wherever one of the pills is thrown, chanting the above mantra, there the whole animal life falls into deep slumber.
AS-14.3.18.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 18 (AS-14.3.18)

AS-14.3.19.text: Following the same procedure, one should separately bury in cremation grounds three white and three black dart-like hairs (salyaka) of a porcupine. When, having on the next fourteenth day taken them out, one throws them together with the ashes of a burnt corpse, chanting the above mantra, the whole animal life in that place falls into deep slumber.
AS-14.3.19.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 19 (AS-14.3.19)

AS-14.3.2.text: One is the eye of a boar; another is that of a khadyota (fire-fly), or a crow, or a mina bird. Having anointed one's own eyes with the above, one can clearly see things at night.
AS-14.3.2.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 2 (AS-14.3.2)

AS-14.3.20.text: I bow to the goddess Suvarnapushpi and to Brahmáni, to the god Bráhma, and to Kusadhvaja; I bow to all serpents and goddesses; I bow to all ascetics.
AS-14.3.20.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 20 (AS-14.3.20)

AS-14.3.21.text: May all Bráhmans and Kshattriyas come under my power; may all Vaisyas and, Súdras be at my beck and call,
AS-14.3.21.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 21 (AS-14.3.21)

AS-14.3.22.text: Oblation to thee, O, Amile, Kimile, Vayujáre, Prayoge, Phake, Kavayusve, Vihále, and Dantakatake, oblation to thee.
AS-14.3.22.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 22 (AS-14.3.22)

AS-14.3.23.text: May the dogs which are anxiously keeping watch over the village fall into deep and happy slumber; these three white dart-like hairs of the porcupine are the creation of Bráhma.
AS-14.3.23.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 23 (AS-14.3.23)

AS-14.3.24.text: All prophets (siddha) have fallen into deep slumber. I do cause sleep to the whole village as far as its boundary till the sun rises. Oblation!
AS-14.3.24.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 24 (AS-14.3.24)

AS-14.3.25.text: When a man, having fasted for seven nights and secured three white dart-like hairs of a porcupine, makes on the fourteenth day of the dark half of the month oblations into the fire with 108 pieces of the sacrificial fire-wood of khadira (mimosa catechu) and other trees together with honey and clarified butter chanting the above mantra, and when, chanting the same mantra, he buries one of the hairs at the entrance of either a village or a house within it, he causes the whole animal life therein to fall into deep slumber.
AS-14.3.25.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 25 (AS-14.3.25)

AS-14.3.26.text: I bow to Bali, the son of Vairochana, to S'atamáya, S'ambara, Nikumbha, Naraka, Kumbha, Tantukachchha, the great demon;
AS-14.3.26.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 26 (AS-14.3.26)

AS-14.3.27.text: To Armálava, Pramíla, Mandolúka, Ghatodbala, to Krishna with his followers, and to the famous woman, Paulomi.
AS-14.3.27.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 27 (AS-14.3.27)

AS-14.3.28.text: Chanting the sacred mantras, I do take the pith or the bone of the corpse (savasárika) productive of my desired ends--may S'alaka demons be victorious; salutation to them; oblation!--May the dogs which are anxiously keeping watch over the village fall into deep and happy slumber.
AS-14.3.28.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 28 (AS-14.3.28)

AS-14.3.29.text: May all prophets (siddhártháh) fall into happy sleep about the object which we are seeking from sunset to sunrise and till the attainment of my desired end. Oblation!
AS-14.3.29.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 29 (AS-14.3.29)

AS-14.3.3.text: Having fasted for three nights, one should, on the day of the star, Pushya, catch hold of the skull of a man who has been killed with a weapon or put to the gallows. Having filled the skull with soil and barley seeds, one should irrigate them with the milk of goats and sheep. Putting on the garland formed of the sprouts of the above barley crop, one can walk invisible to others.
AS-14.3.3.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 3 (AS-14.3.3)

AS-14.3.30.text: Having fasted for four nights and having on the fourteenth day of the dark half of the month performed animal sacrifice (bali) in cremation grounds, one should, repeating the above mantra, collect the pith of a corpse (savasárika) and keep it in a basket made of leaves (pattrapauttaliká). When this basket, being pierced in the centre by a dart-like hair of a porcupine, is buried, chanting the above mantra, the whole animal life therein falls into deep slumber.
AS-14.3.30.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 30 (AS-14.3.30)

AS-14.3.31.text: I take refuge with the god of fire and with all the goddesses in the ten quarters; may all obstructions vanish and may all things come under my power. Oblation.
AS-14.3.31.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 31 (AS-14.3.31)

AS-14.3.32.text: Having fasted for three nights and having on the day of the star of Pushya prepared twenty-one pieces of sugar-candy, one should make oblation into the fire with honey and clarified butter; and having worshipped the pieces of sugar-candy with scents and garlands of flowers, one should bury them. When, having on the next day of the star of Pushya unearthed the pieces of sugar-candy, and chanting the above mantra, one strikes the door-panel of a house with one piece and throws four pieces in the interior, the door will open itself.
AS-14.3.32.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 32 (AS-14.3.32)

AS-14.3.33.text: Having fasted for four nights, one should on the fourteenth day of the dark half of the month get a figure of a bull prepared from the bone of a man, and worship it, repeating the above mantra. Then a cart drawn by two bulls will be brought before the worshipper who can (mount it and) drive in the sky and tell all that is connected with the sun and other planets of the sky.
AS-14.3.33.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 33 (AS-14.3.33)

AS-14.3.34.text: O, Chandáli Kumbhi, Tumba Katuka, and Sárigha, thou art possessed of the bhaga of a woman, oblation to thee.
AS-14.3.34.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 34 (AS-14.3.34)

AS-14.3.35.text: When this mantra is repeated, the door will open and the inmates fall into sleep.
AS-14.3.35.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 35 (AS-14.3.35)

AS-14.3.36.text: Having fasted for three nights, one should on the day of the star of Pushya fill with soil the skull of a man killed with weapons or put to the gallows, and, planting in it valli (vallari ?) plants, should irrigate them with water. Having taken up the grown-up plants on the next day of the star of Pushya (i.e., after 27 days), one should manufacture a rope from them. When this rope is cut into two pieces before a drawn bow or any other shooting machine, the string of those machines will be suddenly cut into two pieces.
AS-14.3.36.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 36 (AS-14.3.36)

AS-14.3.37.text: When the slough of a water-snake (udakáhi) is filled with the breathed-out dirt (uchchhvásamrittika?) of a man or woman (and is held before the face and nose of any person), it causes those organs to swell.
AS-14.3.37.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 37 (AS-14.3.37)

AS-14.3.38.text: When the sack-like skin of the abdomen of a dog or a boar is filled with the breathed-out dirt (uchchhvásamrittika) of a man or woman and is bound (to the body of a man) with the ligaments of a monkey, it causes the man's body to grow in width and length (ánáha),
AS-14.3.38.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 38 (AS-14.3.38)

AS-14.3.39.text: When the figure of an enemy carved out of rájavriksha (cassia fistula) is besmeared with the bile of a brown cow killed with a weapon on the fourteenth day of the dark half of the month, it causes blindness (to the enemy).
AS-14.3.39.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 39 (AS-14.3.39)

AS-14.3.4.text: Having fasted for three nights and having afterwards pulled out on the day of the star of Pushya both the right and the left eyes of a dog, a cat, an owl, and a váguli (?), one should reduce them to two kinds of powder. Then having anointed one's own eyes with this ointment as usual, one can walk invisible to others.
AS-14.3.4.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 4 (AS-14.3.4)

AS-14.3.40.text: Having fasted for four nights and offered animal sacrifice (bali) on the fourteenth day of the dark half of the month, one should get a few bolt-like pieces prepared from the bone of a man put to the gallows. When one of these pieces is put in the feces or urine (of an enemy), it causes (his) body to grow in size (ánáha); and when the same piece is buried under the feet or seat (of an enemy), it causes death by consumption; and when it is buried in the shop, fields, or the house (of an enemy), it causes him loss of livelihood.
AS-14.3.40.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 40 (AS-14.3.40)

AS-14.3.41.text: The same process of smearing and burying holds good with the bolt-like pieces (kílaka) prepared from vidyuddanda tree.
AS-14.3.41.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 41 (AS-14.3.41)

AS-14.3.42.text: When the nail of the little finger (punarnavam aváchínam ?) nimba (nimba melia), káma (bdellium), madhu (celtis orientalis), the hair of a monkey, and the bone of a man, all wound round with the garment of a dead man.
AS-14.3.42.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 42 (AS-14.3.42)

AS-14.3.43.text: Is buried in the house of, or is trodden down by, a man, that man with his wife, children and wealth will not survive three fortnights.
AS-14.3.43.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 43 (AS-14.3.43)

AS-14.3.44.text: When the nail of the little finger, nimba (nimba melia), káma (bdellium), madhu (celtis orientalis), and the bone of a man dead from natural causes are buried under the feet of,
AS-14.3.44.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 44 (AS-14.3.44)

AS-14.3.45.text: Or near the house of, a man or in the vicinity of the camp of an army, of a village, or of a city, that man (or the body of men) with wife, children, and wealth will not survive three fortnights.
AS-14.3.45.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 45 (AS-14.3.45)

AS-14.3.46.text: When the hair of a sheep and a monkey, of a cat and mongoose, of Bráhmans, of low-caste men (svapáka), and of a crow and an owl is collected,
AS-14.3.46.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 46 (AS-14.3.46)

AS-14.3.47.text: And is made into a paste with fæces (vishtávakshunna), its application brings on instantaneous death. When a flower garland of a dead body, the ferment derived from burning corpse, the hair of a mangoose,
AS-14.3.47.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 47 (AS-14.3.47)

AS-14.3.48.text: And the skin of scorpion, a bee, and a snake are buried under the feet of a man, that man will lose all human appearance so long as they are not removed.
AS-14.3.48.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 48 (AS-14.3.48)

AS-14.3.49.text: Having fasted for three nights and having on the day of the star of Pushya planted gunja seeds in the skull, filled with soil, of a man killed with weapons or put to the gallows, one should irrigate it with water. On the new or full moon day with the star of Pushya, one should take out the plants when grown, and prepare out of them circular pedestals (mandaliká). When vessels containing food and water are placed on these pedestals, the food stuffs will never decrease in quantity.
AS-14.3.49.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 49 (AS-14.3.49)

AS-14.3.5.text: Having fasted for three nights, one should, on the day of the star of Pushya, prepare a round-headed pin (saláká) from the branch of purushagháti (punnága tree). Then having filled with ointment (anjana) the skull of any of the animals which roam at nights, and having inserted that skull in the organ of procreation of a dead woman, one should burn it. Having taken it out on the day of the star of Pushya and having anointed one's own eyes with that ointment, one can walk invisible to others.
AS-14.3.5.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 5 (AS-14.3.5)

AS-14.3.50.text: When a grand procession is being celebrated at night, one should cut off the nipples of the udder of a dead cow and burn them in a torch-light flame. A fresh vessel should be plastered in the interior with the paste prepared from these burnt nipples, mixed with the urine of a bull. When this vessel, taken round the village in circumambulation from right to left, is placed below, the whole quantity of the butter produced by all the cows (of the village) will collect itself in the vessel.
AS-14.3.50.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 50 (AS-14.3.50)

AS-14.3.51.text: On the fourteenth day of the dark half of the month combined with the star of Pushya, one should thrust into the organ of procreation of a dog or heat an iron seal (kataláyasam mudrikam) and take it up when it falls down of itself. When, with this seal in hand, a collection of fruits is called out, it will come of itself (before the magician).
AS-14.3.51.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 51 (AS-14.3.51)

AS-14.3.52.text: By the power of mantras, drugs, and other magical performances, one should protect one's own people and hurt those of the enemy.
AS-14.3.52.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 52 (AS-14.3.52)

AS-14.3.6.text: Wherever one may happen to see the corpse burnt or just being burnt of a Bráhman who kept sacrificial fire (while alive), there one should fast for three nights; and having on the day of the star of Pushya formed a sack from the garment of the corpse of a man who has died from natural causes, and having filled the sack with the ashes of the Bráhman's corpse, one may put on the sack on one's back, and walk invisible to others.
AS-14.3.6.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 6 (AS-14.3.6)

AS-14.3.7.text: The slough of a snake filled with the powder of the bones and marrow or fat of the cow sacrificed during the funeral rites of a Bráhman, can, when put on the back of cattle, render them invisible.
AS-14.3.7.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 7 (AS-14.3.7)

AS-14.3.8.text: The slough of prachaláka (a bird?) filled with the ashes of the corpse of a man dead from snake-bite, can render beasts (mriga) invisible.
AS-14.3.8.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 8 (AS-14.3.8)

AS-14.3.9.text: The slough of a snake (ahi) filled with the powder of the bone of the knee-joint mixed with that of the tail and dung (purísha) of an owl and a váguli (?), can render birds invisible.
AS-14.3.9.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 3, Sutra 9 (AS-14.3.9)

AS-14.4.1.text: WITH regard to remedies against poisons and poisonous compounds applied by an enemy against one's own army or people:--
AS-14.4.1.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 1 (AS-14.4.1)

AS-14.4.10.text: The proportion of a dose is as much as an aksha (?) to men; twice as much to cows and horses; and four times as much to elephants and camels.
AS-14.4.10.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 10 (AS-14.4.10)

AS-14.4.11.text: A round ball (mani) prepared from the above mixture and containing gold (rukma) in its centre, removes the the effects due to any kind of poison.
AS-14.4.11.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 11 (AS-14.4.11)

AS-14.4.12.text: A round ball (mani) prepared from the wood of asvattha (holy fig tree) growing wound round with the plants such as jívantí (a medicinal plant), sveta (andropogan aciculatum) the flower of mushkaka (a species of tree), and vanadáka (epidendrum tesseloides), removes the effects due to any kind of poison.
AS-14.4.12.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 12 (AS-14.4.12)

AS-14.4.13.text: The sound of trumpets painted with the above mixture destroys poison; whoever looks at a flag or banner besmeared with the above mixture will get rid of poison.
AS-14.4.13.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 13 (AS-14.4.13)

AS-14.4.14.text: Having applied these remedies to secure the safety of himself and his army, a king should make use of poisonous smokes and other mixtures to vitiate water against his enemy.
AS-14.4.14.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 14 (AS-14.4.14)

AS-14.4.2.text: When the things that are meant for the king's use, inclusive of the limbs of women, as well as the things of the army are washed in the tepid water prepared from the decoction of sleshmátaki (sebesten or cordia myk), kapi (emblica officinalis), madanti (?), danta (ivory), satha (Citron tree), gojigi (gojihva ?--elephantophus scaber), visha (aconitum ferox), pátali (bignonia suave olens), bala (lida cardifolia et rombifolia), syonáka (bignonia indica), punarnava (?), sveta (andropogon aciculatum), and tagara (tabernæmontana coronaria), mixed with chandana (sandal) and the blood of salávriki (jackal), it removes the bad effects of poison.
AS-14.4.2.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 2 (AS-14.4.2)

AS-14.4.3.text: The mixture prepared from the biles of prishata (red-spotted deer), nakula (mongoose), nílakantha (peacock), and godhá (alligator), with charcoal powder (mashíráji), combined with the sprouts (agra) of sinduvára (vitex trifolia), tagara (tabernæmontana coronaria, varuna) (teriandium indicum), tandulíyaka (amaranthus polygamus), and sataparva (convolvulus repens) together with pindítaka (vangueria spinosa) removes the effects of the mixture of madana.
AS-14.4.3.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 3 (AS-14.4.3)

AS-14.4.4.text: Among the decoctions of the roots of srigála (bignonia indica), vinna (?), madana, sinduvára (vitex trifolia), tagara (tabernæmontana coronaria), and valli, (a creeper ?), any one or all mixed with milk removes, when drunk, the effects of the mixture of madana.
AS-14.4.4.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 4 (AS-14.4.4)

AS-14.4.5.text: The stinking oil extracted from kaidarya (vangueria spinosa) removes madness.
AS-14.4.5.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 5 (AS-14.4.5)

AS-14.4.6.text: The mixture prepared from priyangu (panic seed) and naktamála (galedupa arborea) removes, when applied through the nose, leprosy.
AS-14.4.6.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 6 (AS-14.4.6)

AS-14.4.7.text: The mixture prepared from kushtha (costus) and lodhra (symplocus) removes consumption.
AS-14.4.7.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 7 (AS-14.4.7)

AS-14.4.8.text: The mixture prepared from katuphala (glelina arborea), dravanti (anthericum tuberosum), and vilanga (a kind of seed) removes, when applied through the nose, headache and other diseases of the head.
AS-14.4.8.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 8 (AS-14.4.8)

AS-14.4.9.text: The application of the mixture prepared from priyangu (panic seed), manjishtha (rubia manjit), tagara (tabernæmontana coronaria), lákshárasa (the juice or essence of lac) madhuka (?), haridrá (turmeric), and kshaudra (honey) to persons who have fallen senseless by being beaten by a rope, by falling into water, or by eating poison, or by being whipped, or by falling, resuscitates them.
AS-14.4.9.label: Arthashastra Book 14, Chapter 4, Sutra 9 (AS-14.4.9)

AS-15.1.1.text: THE subsistence of mankind is termed artha, wealth; the earth which contains mankind is also termed artha, wealth; that science which treats of the means of acquiring and maintaining the earth is the Arthasástra, Science of Polity.
AS-15.1.1.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 1 (AS-15.1.1)

AS-15.1.10.text: Explanation in detached words is the mentioning of a fact in detail; for example: "Absence of discrepancy in the perception of sound, touch, colour, flavour, and scent by means of the ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose, is what is meant by restraint of the organs of sense."
AS-15.1.10.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 10 (AS-15.1.10)

AS-15.1.11.text: Such statement as "Thus one should live," is guidance; for example: "Not violating the laws of righteousness and economy, he should live."
AS-15.1.11.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 11 (AS-15.1.11)

AS-15.1.12.text: Such statement, as ‘he says thus,’ is a quotation; for example: "The school of Manu say that a king should make his assembly of ministers consist of twelve ministers; the school of Brihaspati say that it should consist of sixteen ministers; the school of Usans say it should contain twenty members; but Kautilya holds that it should contain as many ministers as the need of the kingdom requires.”
AS-15.1.12.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 12 (AS-15.1.12)

AS-15.1.13.text: When a rule dwelt upon in connection with a question is said to apply to another question also, it is termed application; for example: "What is said of a debt not repaid holds good with failure to make good a promised gift."
AS-15.1.13.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 13 (AS-15.1.13)

AS-15.1.14.text: Establishing a fact by what is to be treated of later on is ‘place of reference;’ for example: "By making use of such strategic means as conciliation, bribery, dissension, and coercion, as we shall explain in connection with calamities."
AS-15.1.14.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 14 (AS-15.1.14)

AS-15.1.15.text: Proving an unseen thing or course of circumstances by what has been seen is simile; for example: "Like a father his son, he should protect those of his subjects who have passed the period of the remission of taxes."
AS-15.1.15.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 15 (AS-15.1.15)

AS-15.1.16.text: What naturally follows from a statement of facts, though not spoken of in plain terms, is implication; for example, "Whoever has full experience of the affairs of this world should, through the medium of the courtiers and other friends, win the favour of a king who is of good character and worthy sovereign. It follows from this that no one should seek the favour of a king through the medium of the king's enemies."
AS-15.1.16.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 16 (AS-15.1.16)

AS-15.1.17.text: When the statement of a reason is equally applicable to two cases of circumstances, it is termed doubt; for example: "Which of the two should a conqueror march against: one whose subjects are impoverished and greedy, or one whose subjects are oppressed?"
AS-15.1.17.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 17 (AS-15.1.17)

AS-15.1.18.text: When the nature of procedure to be specified in connection with a thing is said to be equal to what has already been specified in connection with another, it is termed reference to similar procedure; for example: "On the lands allotted to him for the purpose of carrying on agricultural operations, he should do as before."
AS-15.1.18.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 18 (AS-15.1.18)

AS-15.1.19.text: The inference of a reverse statement from a positive statement is termed contrariety; for example: "The reverse will be the appearance of a king who is not pleased with the messenger."
AS-15.1.19.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 19 (AS-15.1.19)

AS-15.1.20.text: That portion of a sentence which is omitted, though necessary to convey a complete sense, is ellipsis; for example: "With his feathers plucked off, he will lose his power to move." Here ‘like a bird’ is omitted.
AS-15.1.20.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 20 (AS-15.1.20)

AS-15.1.21.text: When the opinion of another person is stated but not refuted, it is acceptance of that opinion; for example: “Wings, front, and reserve, is the form of an array of the army according to the school of Usanas.”
AS-15.1.21.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 21 (AS-15.1.21)

AS-15.1.22.text: Description in detail is explanation; for example: "Especially amongst assemblies and confederacies of kings possessing the characteristics of assemblies, quarrel is due to gambling ; and destruction of persons due to the quarrel. Hence, among evil propensities, gambling is the worst evil, since it renders the king powerless for activity."
AS-15.1.22.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 22 (AS-15.1.22)

AS-15.1.23.text: Stating the derivative sense of a word, is derivation; for example: "That which throws off (vyasyati) a king from his prosperous career is propensity (vyasana).
AS-15.1.23.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 23 (AS-15.1.23)

AS-15.1.24.text: The mentioning of a fact to illustrate a statement, is illustration; for example: "In war with a superior, the inferior will be reduced to the same condition as that of a foot-soldier fighting with an elephant."
AS-15.1.24.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 24 (AS-15.1.24)

AS-15.1.25.text: Removal of an undesired implication from a statement is exception; for example: "A king may allow his enemy's army to be present close to his territory, unless he suspects of the existence of any internal trouble."
AS-15.1.25.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 25 (AS-15.1.25)

AS-15.1.26.text: Words which are not used by others in the special sense in which they are used by the author are his own technical terms; for example: "He who is close to the conqueror's territory is the first member; next to him comes the second member; and next to the second comes the third."
AS-15.1.26.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 26 (AS-15.1.26)

AS-15.1.27.text: The citation of another's opinion to be refuted, is prima facie view; for example: "Of the two evils, the distress of the king and that of his minister, the latter is worse."
AS-15.1.27.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 27 (AS-15.1.27)

AS-15.1.28.text: Settled opinion is rejoinder; for example: "The distress of the king is worse, since everything depends upon him; for the king is the central pivot, as it were."
AS-15.1.28.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 28 (AS-15.1.28)

AS-15.1.29.text: That which is universal in its application is conclusion or an established fact: for example: "A king should ever be ready for manly effort."
AS-15.1.29.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 29 (AS-15.1.29)

AS-15.1.3.text: the book (adhikarana), contents (vidhána), suggestion of similar facts (yoga), the meaning of a word (padártha), the purport of reason (hetvartha), mention of a fact in brief (uddesa), mention of a fact in detail (nirdesa), guidance (upadesa), quotation, (apadesa), application (atidesa) the place of reference (pradesa), simile (upamána), implication (arthápatti), doubt (samsaya), reference to similar procedure (presanga), contrariety (viparyaya), ellipsis (vakyasesha), acceptance (anumata), explanation (vyákhayána), derivation (nirvachana), illustration (nidarsana), exception (apavarga), the author’s own technical terms (svasanjá), prima facie view (púrva paksha), rejoinder (uttrapaksha), conclusion (ekánta), reference to a subsequent portion (anágatávekshana), reference to a previous portion (atikrantávekshana), command (niyoga), alternative (vikalpa), compounding together (samuchchaya), and determinable fact (úhya).
AS-15.1.3.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 3 (AS-15.1.3)

AS-15.1.30.text: Drawing attention to a later chapter is reference to a subsequent portion; for example: "We shall explain balance and weights in the chapter, ‘The Superintendent of Weights and Measures’."
AS-15.1.30.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 30 (AS-15.1.30)

AS-15.1.31.text: The statement that it has been already spoken of is reference to a previous portion: for example, "The qualifications of a minister have already been described."
AS-15.1.31.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 31 (AS-15.1.31)

AS-15.1.32.text: ‘Thus and not otherwise’ is command; for example: "Hence he should be taught the laws of righteousness and wealth, but not unrighteousness and non-wealth."
AS-15.1.32.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 32 (AS-15.1.32)

AS-15.1.33.text: ‘This or that’ is alternative; for example: "or daughters born of approved marriage (dharmaviváha)."
AS-15.1.33.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 33 (AS-15.1.33)

AS-15.1.34.text: ‘Both with this and that’ is compounding together; for example: "Whoever is begotten by a man on his wife is agnatic both to the father and the father's relatives."
AS-15.1.34.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 34 (AS-15.1.34)

AS-15.1.35.text: That which is to be determined after consideration is determinable fact; for example: "Experts shall determine the validity or invalidity of gifts so that neither the giver nor the receiver is likely to be hurt thereby."
AS-15.1.35.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 35 (AS-15.1.35)

AS-15.1.36.text: Thus this Sástra, conforming to these paragraphic divisions is composed as a guide to acquire and secure this and the other world.
AS-15.1.36.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 36 (AS-15.1.36)

AS-15.1.37.text: In the light of this Sástra one cannot only set on foot righteous, economical, and aesthetical acts and maintain them, but also put down unrighteous, uneconomical and displeasing acts.
AS-15.1.37.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 37 (AS-15.1.37)

AS-15.1.38.text: This Sástra has been made by him who from intolerance (of misrule) quickly rescued the scriptures and the science of weapons and the earth which had passed to the Nanda king.
AS-15.1.38.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 38 (AS-15.1.38)

AS-15.1.39.text: Having seen discrepancies in many ways on the part of the writers of commentaries on the Sástras, Vishnu Gupta himself has made (this) Sútra and commentary.
AS-15.1.39.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 39 (AS-15.1.39)

AS-15.1.4.text: That portion of a work in which a subject or topic is treated of is a book, as for example: “This Arthasástra or Science of Polity has been made as a compendium of all those Arthasástras which, as a guidance to kings in acquiring and maintaining the earth, have been written by ancient teachers.”
AS-15.1.4.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 4 (AS-15.1.4)

AS-15.1.5.text: A brief description of the matter contained in a book is its contents, as: "the end of learning; association with the aged; control of the organs of sense; the creation of ministers, and the like."
AS-15.1.5.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 5 (AS-15.1.5)

AS-15.1.6.text: Pointing out similar facts by the use of such words as ‘These and the like,’ is suggestion of similar facts; for example: "The world consisting of the four castes and the four religious divisions and the like."
AS-15.1.6.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 6 (AS-15.1.6)

AS-15.1.7.text: The sense which a word has to convey is its meaning; for example, with regard to the words múlahara: "Whoever squanders the wealth acquired for him by his father and grandfather is a múlahara, prodigal son."
AS-15.1.7.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 7 (AS-15.1.7)

AS-15.1.8.text: What is meant to prove an assertion is the purport of reason; for example: "For charity and enjoyment of life depend upon wealth."
AS-15.1.8.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 8 (AS-15.1.8)

AS-15.1.9.text: Saying in one word is mentioning a fact in brief; for example: "It is the control of the organs of sense on which success in learning and discipline depend."
AS-15.1.9.label: Arthashastra Book 15, Chapter 1, Sutra 9 (AS-15.1.9)

AS-2.1.1.text: EITHER by inducing foreigners to immigrate (paradesapraváhanena) or by causing the thickly-populated centres of his own kingdom to send forth the excessive population (svadésábhishyandavámanéna vá), the king may construct villages either on new sites or on old ruins (bhútapúrvama vá).
AS-2.1.1.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 1 (AS-2.1.1)

AS-2.1.10.text: The king shall bestow on cultivators only such favour and remission (anugrahaparihárau) as will tend to swell the treasury, and shall avoid such as will deplete it.
AS-2.1.10.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 10 (AS-2.1.10)

AS-2.1.11.text: A king with depleted treasury will eat into the very vitality of both citizens and country people. Either on the occasion of opening new settlements or on any other emergent occasions, remission of taxes shall be made.
AS-2.1.11.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 11 (AS-2.1.11)

AS-2.1.12.text: He shall regard with fatherly kindness those who have passed the period of remission of taxes.
AS-2.1.12.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 12 (AS-2.1.12)

AS-2.1.13.text: He shall carry on mining operations and manufactures, exploit timber and elephant forests, offer facilities for cattlebreeding and commerce, construct roads for traffic both by land and water, and set up market towns (panyapattana).
AS-2.1.13.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 13 (AS-2.1.13)

AS-2.1.14.text: He shall also construct reservoirs (sétu) filled with water either perennial or drawn from some other source. Or he may provide with sites, roads, timber, and other necessary things those who construct reservoirs of their own accord. Likewise in the construction of places of pilgrimage (punyasthána) and of groves.
AS-2.1.14.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 14 (AS-2.1.14)

AS-2.1.15.text: Whoever stays away from any kind of cooperative construction (sambhúya setubhandhát) shall send his servants and bullocks to carry on his work, shall have a share in the expenditure, but shall have no claim to the profit.
AS-2.1.15.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 15 (AS-2.1.15)

AS-2.1.16.text: The king shall exercise his right of ownership (swámyam) with regard to fishing, ferrying and trading in vegetables (haritapanya) in reservoirs or lakes (sétushu).
AS-2.1.16.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 16 (AS-2.1.16)

AS-2.1.17.text: Those who do not heed the claims of their slaves (dása), hirelings (áhitaka), and relatives shall be taught their duty.
AS-2.1.17.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 17 (AS-2.1.17)

AS-2.1.18.text: The king shall provide the orphans, (bála), the aged, the infirm, the afflicted, and the helpless with maintenance. He shall also provide subsistence to helpless women when they are carrying and also to the children they give birth to.
AS-2.1.18.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 18 (AS-2.1.18)

AS-2.1.19.text: Elders among the villagers shall improve the property of bereaved minors till the latter attain their age; so also the property of Gods.
AS-2.1.19.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 19 (AS-2.1.19)

AS-2.1.2.text: Villages consisting each of not less than a hundred families and of not more than five-hundred families of agricultural people of súdra caste, with boundaries extending as far as a krósa (2250 yds.) or two, and capable of protecting each other shall be formed. Boundaries shall be denoted by a river, a mountain, forests, bulbous plants (grishti), caves, artificial buildings (sétubandha), or by trees such as sálmali (silk cotton tree), samí (Acacia Suma), and kshíravriksha (milky trees).
AS-2.1.2.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 2 (AS-2.1.2)

AS-2.1.20.text: When a capable person other than an apostate (patita) or mother neglects to maintain his or her child, wife, mother, father, minor brothers, sisters, or widowed girls (kanyá vidhaváscha), he or she shall be punished with a fine of twelve panas.
AS-2.1.20.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 20 (AS-2.1.20)

AS-2.1.21.text: When, without making provision for the maintenance of his wife and sons, any person embraces ascetism, he shall be punished with the first amercement; likewise any person who converts a woman to ascetism (pravrájayatah).
AS-2.1.21.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 21 (AS-2.1.21)

AS-2.1.22.text: Whoever has passed the age of copulation may become an ascetic after distributing the properties of his own acquisition (among his sons); otherwise, he will be punished.
AS-2.1.22.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 22 (AS-2.1.22)

AS-2.1.23.text: No ascetic other than a vánaprastha (forest-hermit), no company other than the one of local birth (sajátádanyassanghah), and no guilds of any kind other than local cooperative guilds (sámuttháyiká- danyassamayánubandhah) shall find entrance into the villages of the kingdom. Nor shall there be in villages buildings (sáláh) intended for sports and plays. Nor, in view of procuring money, free labour, commodities, grains, and liquids in plenty, shall actors, dancers, singers, drummers, buffoons (vágjívana), and bards (kusílava) make any disturbance to the work of the villagers; for helpless villagers are always dependent and bent upon their fields.
AS-2.1.23.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 23 (AS-2.1.23)

AS-2.1.24.text: The king shall avoid taking possession of any country which is liable to the inroads of enemies and wild tribes and which is harassed by frequent visitations of famine and pestilence. He shall also keep away from expensive sports.
AS-2.1.24.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 24 (AS-2.1.24)

AS-2.1.25.text: He shall protect agriculture from the molestation of oppressive fines, free labour, and taxes (dandavishtikarábádhaih); herds of cattle from thieves, tigers, poisonous creatures and cattle-disease.
AS-2.1.25.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 25 (AS-2.1.25)

AS-2.1.26.text: He shall not only clear roads of traffic from the molestations of courtiers (vallabha), of workmen (kármika), of robbers, and of boundary-guards, but also keep them from being destroyed by herds of cattle.
AS-2.1.26.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 26 (AS-2.1.26)

AS-2.1.27.text: Thus the king shall not only keep in good repair timber and elephant forests, buildings, and mines created in the past, but also set up new ones.
AS-2.1.27.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 27 (AS-2.1.27)

AS-2.1.3.text: There shall be set up a stháníya (a fortress of that name) in the centre of eight-hundred villages, a drónamukha in the centre of four-hundred villages, a khárvátika in the centre of two-hundred villages and sangrahana in the midst of a collection of ten villages.
AS-2.1.3.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 3 (AS-2.1.3)

AS-2.1.4.text: There shall be constructed in the extremities of the kingdom forts manned by boundary-guards (antapála) whose duty shall be to guard the entrances into the kingdom. The interior of the kingdom shall be watched by trap-keepers (vágurika), archers (sábara), hunters (pulinda), chandálas, and wild tribes (aranyachára).
AS-2.1.4.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 4 (AS-2.1.4)

AS-2.1.5.text: Those who perform sacrifices (ritvik), spiritual guides, priests, and those learned in the Vedas shall be granted Brahmadaya lands yielding sufficient produce and exempted from taxes and fines (adandkaráni).
AS-2.1.5.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 5 (AS-2.1.5)

AS-2.1.6.text: Superintendents, Accountants, Gopas, Sthánikas, Veterinary Surgeons (Aníkastha), physicians, horse-trainers, and messengers shall also be endowed with lands which they shall have no right to alienate by sale or mortgage.
AS-2.1.6.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 6 (AS-2.1.6)

AS-2.1.7.text: Lands prepared for cultivation shall be given to tax- payers (karada) only for life (ekapurushikáni).
AS-2.1.7.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 7 (AS-2.1.7)

AS-2.1.8.text: Unprepared lands shall not be taken away from those who are preparing them for cultivation.
AS-2.1.8.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 8 (AS-2.1.8)

AS-2.1.9.text: Lands may be confiscated from those who do not cultivate them; and given to others; or they may be cultivated by village labourers (grámabhritaka) and traders (vaidehaka), lest those owners who do not properly cultivate them might pay less (to the government). If cultivators pay their taxes easily, they may be favourably supplied with grains, cattle, and money.
AS-2.1.9.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 1, Sutra 9 (AS-2.1.9)

AS-2.10.1.text: (TEACHERS) say that (the word) sásana, command, (is applicable only to) royal writs (sásana).
AS-2.10.1.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 1 (AS-2.10.1)

AS-2.10.10.text: Avoidance of redundancy or deficiency in words or letters; impressive description of subject matter by citing reasons, examples, and illustrations; and the use of appropriate and suitably strong words (asrántapada) is completeness.
AS-2.10.10.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 10 (AS-2.10.10)

AS-2.10.11.text: The description in exquisite style of a good purport with a pleasing effect is sweetness.
AS-2.10.11.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 11 (AS-2.10.11)

AS-2.10.12.text: The use of words other than colloquial (agrámya) is dignity.
AS-2.10.12.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 12 (AS-2.10.12)

AS-2.10.13.text: The alphabetical letters beginning with Akára are sixty-three.
AS-2.10.13.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 13 (AS-2.10.13)

AS-2.10.14.text: The combination of letters is a word (pada). The word is of four kinds—nouns, verbs, prefixes of verbs, and particles (nipáta).
AS-2.10.14.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 14 (AS-2.10.14)

AS-2.10.15.text: A verb is that which has no definite gender and signifies an action.
AS-2.10.15.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 15 (AS-2.10.15)

AS-2.10.16.text: A group of words conveying a complete sense is a sentence (vákya).
AS-2.10.16.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 16 (AS-2.10.16)

AS-2.10.17.text: Combination of words (varga) consisting of not more than three words and not less than one word shall be so formed as to harmonise with the meaning of immediately following words.
AS-2.10.17.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 17 (AS-2.10.17)

AS-2.10.18.text: The word, ‘iti,’ is used to indicate the completion of a writ; and also to indicate an oral message as in the phrase ‘váchikamasyeti,’ an oral message along with this (writ).
AS-2.10.18.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 18 (AS-2.10.18)

AS-2.10.19.text: Calumniation (nindá), commendation, inquiry, narration request, refusal, censure, prohibition, command, conciliation, promise of help, threat, and persuasion are the thirteen purposes for which writs are issued.
AS-2.10.19.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 19 (AS-2.10.19)

AS-2.10.2.text: Writs are of great importance to kings inasmuch as treaties and ultimate leading to war depend upon writs.
AS-2.10.2.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 2 (AS-2.10.2)

AS-2.10.20.text: Calumniation (nindá) consists in speaking ill of one's family, body and acts.
AS-2.10.20.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 20 (AS-2.10.20)

AS-2.10.21.text: Commendation (prasamsá) consists in praising one's family, person, and acts.
AS-2.10.21.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 21 (AS-2.10.21)

AS-2.10.22.text: To say that 'it is not worthy of thee,' is censure (upálambhah).
AS-2.10.22.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 22 (AS-2.10.22)

AS-2.10.23.text: To say 'what I am, thou art that; whichever article is mine is thine also, is conciliation (sántvam).
AS-2.10.23.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 23 (AS-2.10.23)

AS-2.10.24.text: To hold out help in trouble is promise of help (abhyavapattih).
AS-2.10.24.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 24 (AS-2.10.24)

AS-2.10.25.text: Pointing out the evil consequences that may occur in future is threat (abhibartsanam).
AS-2.10.25.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 25 (AS-2.10.25)

AS-2.10.26.text: Persuasion is of three kinds: that made for the purpose of money, that made in case of one's failure to fulfill a promise, and that made on occasion of any trouble.
AS-2.10.26.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 26 (AS-2.10.26)

AS-2.10.27.text: Also writs of information, of command, and of gift; likewise writs of remission, of licence, of guidance, of reply, and of general proclamation are other varieties.
AS-2.10.27.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 27 (AS-2.10.27)

AS-2.10.28.text: Thus says (the messenger); so says (the king); if there is any truth in this (statement of the messenger), then the thing (agreed to) should at once be surrendered; (the messenger) has informed the king of all the deeds of the enemy. (Parakára);—this is the writ of information which is held to be of various forms.
AS-2.10.28.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 28 (AS-2.10.28)

AS-2.10.29.text: Wherever and especially regarding Government servants the king's order either for punishment or for rewards is issued, it is called writ of command (ájnálékha).
AS-2.10.29.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 29 (AS-2.10.29)

AS-2.10.3.text: Hence one who is possessed of ministerial qualifications, acquainted with all kinds of customs, smart in composition, good in legible writing, and sharp in reading shall be appointed as a writer (lékhaka).
AS-2.10.3.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 3 (AS-2.10.3)

AS-2.10.30.text: Where the bestowal of honour for deserving merit is contemplated either as help to alleviate affliction (ádhi) or as gift (paridána), there are issued writs of gift (upagrahalekha).
AS-2.10.30.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 30 (AS-2.10.30)

AS-2.10.31.text: Whatever favour (anugraha) to special castes, cities, villages, or countries of various description is announced in obedience to the king's order, it is called writ of remission (pariháralékha) by those who know it.
AS-2.10.31.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 31 (AS-2.10.31)

AS-2.10.32.text: Likewise licence or permission (nisrishti) shall be enjoined either in word or deed; accordingly it is styled verbal order or writ of licence.
AS-2.10.32.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 32 (AS-2.10.32)

AS-2.10.33.text: Various kinds of providential visitations or well ascertained evils of human make are believed to be the cause for issuing writs of guidance (pravrittilékha) to attempt remedies against them.
AS-2.10.33.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 33 (AS-2.10.33)

AS-2.10.34.text: When having read a letter and discussed as to the form of reply thereto, a reply in accordance with the king's order is made, it is called a writ of reply (pratilékha).
AS-2.10.34.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 34 (AS-2.10.34)

AS-2.10.35.text: When the king directs his viceroys (isvara) and other officers to protect and give material help to travellers either on roads or in the interior of the country, it is termed writ of general proclamation (sarvatraga lekha)
AS-2.10.35.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 35 (AS-2.10.35)

AS-2.10.36.text: Negotiation, bribery, causing dissension, and open attack are forms of stratagem (upáya).
AS-2.10.36.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 36 (AS-2.10.36)

AS-2.10.37.text: Praising the qualities (of an enemy), narrating the mutual relationship, pointing out mutual benefit, showing vast future prospects, and identity of interests.
AS-2.10.37.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 37 (AS-2.10.37)

AS-2.10.38.text: When the family, person, occupation, conduct, learning, properties, etc. (of an enemy) are commended with due attention to their worth, it is termed praising the qualities (gunasankírthana).
AS-2.10.38.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 38 (AS-2.10.38)

AS-2.10.39.text: When the fact of having agnates, blood-relations, teachers (maukha), priestly hierarchy (srauva), family, and friends in common is pointed out, it is known as narration of mutual relationship (sambandhópakhyána).
AS-2.10.39.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 39 (AS-2.10.39)

AS-2.10.4.text: Such a writer, having attentively listened to the king's order and having well thought out the matter under consideration, shall reduce the order to writing.
AS-2.10.4.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 4 (AS-2.10.4)

AS-2.10.40.text: When both parties, the party of a king and that of his enemy are shown to be helpful to each other, it is known as pointing out mutual benefit (parasparópakárasamdarsanam).
AS-2.10.40.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 40 (AS-2.10.40)

AS-2.10.41.text: Inducement such as 'this being done thus, such result will accrue to both of us,' is showing vast future prospects (Ayátipradarsanam).
AS-2.10.41.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 41 (AS-2.10.41)

AS-2.10.42.text: To say 'what I am, that thou art; thou mayest utilize in thy works whatever is mine,' is identity of interests (átmópanidhánam).
AS-2.10.42.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 42 (AS-2.10.42)

AS-2.10.43.text: Causing fears and suspicion as well as threatening is known as sowing dissension.
AS-2.10.43.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 43 (AS-2.10.43)

AS-2.10.44.text: Clumsiness, contradiction, repetition, bad grammar, and misarrangement are the faults of a writ.
AS-2.10.44.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 44 (AS-2.10.44)

AS-2.10.45.text: Black and ugly leaf, (kálapatrakamacháru) and uneven and uncoloured (virága) writing cause clumsiness (akánti).
AS-2.10.45.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 45 (AS-2.10.45)

AS-2.10.46.text: Subsequent portion disagreeing with previous portion of a letter, causes contradiction (vyágháta).
AS-2.10.46.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 46 (AS-2.10.46)

AS-2.10.47.text: Stating for a second time what has already been said above is repetition.
AS-2.10.47.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 47 (AS-2.10.47)

AS-2.10.48.text: Wrong use of words in gender, number, time and case is bad grammar (apasabda).
AS-2.10.48.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 48 (AS-2.10.48)

AS-2.10.49.text: Division of paragraphs (varga) in unsuitable places, omission of necessary division of paragraphs, and violation of any other necessary qualities of a writ constitute misarrangement (samplava).
AS-2.10.49.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 49 (AS-2.10.49)

AS-2.10.5.text: As to a writ addressed to a lord (ísvara), it shall contain a polite mention of his country, his possessions, his family and his name, and as to that addressed to a common man (anisvara), it shall make a polite mention of his country and name.
AS-2.10.5.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 5 (AS-2.10.5)

AS-2.10.50.text: Having followed all sciences and having fully observed forms of writing in vogue, these rules of writing royal writs have been laid down by Kautilya in the interest of kings.
AS-2.10.50.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 50 (AS-2.10.50)

AS-2.10.6.text: Having paid sufficient attention to the caste, family, social rank, age, learning (sruta), occupation, property, character (síla), blood-relationship (yaunánubandha) of the addressee, as well as to the place and time (of writing), the writer shall form a writ befitting the position of the person addressed.
AS-2.10.6.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 6 (AS-2.10.6)

AS-2.10.7.text: Arrangement of subject-matter (arthakrama), relevancy (sambandha), completeness, sweetness, dignity, and lucidity are the necessary qualities of a writ.
AS-2.10.7.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 7 (AS-2.10.7)

AS-2.10.8.text: The act of mentioning facts in the order of their importance is arrangement.
AS-2.10.8.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 8 (AS-2.10.8)

AS-2.10.9.text: When subsequent facts are not contradictory to facts just or previously mentioned, and so on till the completion of the letter, it is termed relevancy.
AS-2.10.9.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 10, Sutra 9 (AS-2.10.9)

AS-2.11.1.text: THE Superintendent of the treasury shall, in the presence of qualified persons, admit into the treasury whatever he ought to, gems (ratna) and articles of superior or inferior value.
AS-2.11.1.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 1 (AS-2.11.1)

AS-2.11.10.text: That which contains three slab-like gems (triphalaka) or five slab-like gems (panchaphalaka) in the centre is termed Phalakahára.
AS-2.11.10.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 10 (AS-2.11.10)

AS-2.11.11.text: An only string of pearls is called pure Ekávali; the same with a gem in the centre is called Yashti; the same variegated with gold globules is termed Ratnávali.
AS-2.11.11.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 11 (AS-2.11.11)

AS-2.11.12.text: A string made of pearls and gold globules alternately put is called Apavartaka.
AS-2.11.12.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 12 (AS-2.11.12)

AS-2.11.13.text: Strings of pearls with a gold wire between two strings is called Sopánaka.
AS-2.11.13.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 13 (AS-2.11.13)

AS-2.11.14.text: The above will explain the formation of head-strings, bracelets, anklets, waist-bands, and other varieties.
AS-2.11.14.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 14 (AS-2.11.14)

AS-2.11.15.text: Kauta, that which is obtained in the Kúta; Mauleyaka, that which is found in the Múleya; and Párasamudraka, that which is found beyond the ocean are several varieties of gems.
AS-2.11.15.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 15 (AS-2.11.15)

AS-2.11.16.text: That which possesses such pleasant colour as that of the red lotus flower, or that of the flower of Párijáta (Erithrina Indica), or that of the rising sun is the Saugandhika gem.
AS-2.11.16.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 16 (AS-2.11.16)

AS-2.11.17.text: That which is of the colour of blue lotus flower, or of sirísha (Acacia Sirisa), or of water, or of fresh bamboo, or of the colour of the feathers of a parrot is the Vaidúrya gem Pushyarága, Gómútraka, and Gómédika are other varieties of the same.
AS-2.11.17.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 17 (AS-2.11.17)

AS-2.11.18.text: That which is characterised with blue lines, that which is of the colour of the flower of Kaláya (a kind of phraseolus), or which is intensely blue, which possesses the colour of Jambu fruit (rose apple), or which is as blue as the clouds is the Indraníla gem; Nandaka (pleasing gem), Sravanmadhya (that which appears to pour water from its centre), Sítavrishti (that which appears to pour cold shower), and Súryakánta (sunstone) are other forms of gems.
AS-2.11.18.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 18 (AS-2.11.18)

AS-2.11.19.text: Gems are hexagonal, quadrangular, or circular possessed of dazzling glow, pure, smooth, heavy, brilliant, transparent (antargataprabha) and illuminating; such are the qualities of gems.
AS-2.11.19.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 19 (AS-2.11.19)

AS-2.11.2.text: Támraparnika, that which is produced in the támraparni; Pándyakavátaka, that which is obtained in Pándyakavata; Pásikya, that which is produced in the Pása; Kauleya, that which is produced in the kúla; Chaurneya, that which is produced in the Chúrna; Mahéndra, that which is obtained near the mountain of Mahéndra; Kárdamika, that which is produced in the Kárdama; Srautasíya, that which is produced in the Srótasi; Hrádíya, that which is produced in (a deep pool of water known as) Hrada; and Haimavata, that which is obtained in the vicinity of the Himalayas are the several varieties of pearls.
AS-2.11.2.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 2 (AS-2.11.2)

AS-2.11.20.text: Faint colour, sandy layer, spots, holes, bad perforation, and scratches are the defects of gems.
AS-2.11.20.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 20 (AS-2.11.20)

AS-2.11.21.text: Vimalaka (pure), sasyaka (plant-like), Anjanamúlaka (deep-dark), Pittaka (like the bile of a cow) Sulabhaka (easily procurable), Lohitaka (red), Amritámsuka (of white rays), Jyótírasaka (glowing), Maileyaka, Ahichchhatraka , (procured in the country of Ahichchhatra), Kúrpa, Pútikúrpa, and Sugandhikúrpa, Kshírapaka, Suktichúrnaka (like the powder of an oystershell), Silápraválaka (like coral), Pulaka, Súkrapulaka are varieties of inferior gems.
AS-2.11.21.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 21 (AS-2.11.21)

AS-2.11.22.text: Sabháráshtraka, that which is found in the country of Sabháráshtra; Madhyamaráshtraka, that which is found in the Central Province; Kásmaka, that which is found in the country of Kásmaka; Sríkatanaka, that which is found in the vicinity of the mountain, Vedótkata; Manimantaka, that which is found near the mountain Maniman or Manimanta; and Indravánaká are diamonds.
AS-2.11.22.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 22 (AS-2.11.22)

AS-2.11.23.text: Mines, streams, and other miscellaneous places are their sources.
AS-2.11.23.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 23 (AS-2.11.23)

AS-2.11.24.text: The colour of a diamond may be like that of a cat's eye, that of the flower of Sirísha (Acacia Sirísa), the urine of a cow, the bile of a cow, like alum (sphatika), the flower of Málati, or like that of any of the gems (described above).
AS-2.11.24.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 24 (AS-2.11.24)

AS-2.11.25.text: That which is big, heavy, hard (prahárasaham, tolerant of hitting), regular (samakóna), capable of scratching on the surface of vessels (bhájanalékhi), refractive of light (kubrámi), and brilliant is the best.
AS-2.11.25.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 25 (AS-2.11.25)

AS-2.11.26.text: That which is devoid of angles, uneven (nirasríkam), and bent on one side (pársvápavrittam) is inauspicious.
AS-2.11.26.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 26 (AS-2.11.26)

AS-2.11.27.text: Alakandaka, and Vaivarnaka are the two varieties of coral which is possessed of ruby-like colour, which is very hard, and which is free from the contamination of other substances inside.
AS-2.11.27.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 27 (AS-2.11.27)

AS-2.11.28.text: Sátana is red and smells like the earth; Gósirshaka is dark red and smells like fish; Harichandana is of the colour of the feathers of a parrot and smells like tamarind or mango fruit; likewise Tárnasa; Grámeruka is red or dark red and smells like the urine of a goat; Daivasabheya is red and smells like a lotus flower; likewise Aupaka (Jápaka); Jongaka and Taurupa are red or dark red and soft; Maleyaka is reddish white; Kuchandana is as black as Agaru (resin of the aloe) or red or dark red and very rough; Kála-parvataka is of pleasant appearance; Kosákaraparvataka (that which is the product of that mountain which is of the shape of a bud) is black or variegated black; Sítódakíya is black and soft, and smells like a lotus-flower; Nágaparvataka (that which is the product of Naga mountain) is rough and is possessed of the colour of Saivala (Vallisneria); and Sákala is brown.
AS-2.11.28.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 28 (AS-2.11.28)

AS-2.11.29.text: Light, soft, moist (asyána, not dry), as greasy as ghee, of pleasant smell, adhesive to the skin, of mild smell, retentive of colour and smell, tolerant of heat, absorptive of heat, and comfortable to the skin--these are the characteristics of sandal (chandana).
AS-2.11.29.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 29 (AS-2.11.29)

AS-2.11.3.text: Oyster-shells, conch-shells, and other miscellaneous things are the wombs of pearls.
AS-2.11.3.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 3 (AS-2.11.3)

AS-2.11.30.text: Jongaka is black or variegated black and is possessed of variegated spots; Dongaka is black; and Párasamudraka is of variegated colour and smells like cascus or like Navamálika (jasminum).
AS-2.11.30.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 30 (AS-2.11.30)

AS-2.11.31.text: (Agaru is) heavy, soft, greasy, smells far and long, burns slowly, gives out continuous smoke while burning, is of uniform smell, absorbs heat, and is so adhesive to the skin as not to be removable by rubbing;—these are the characteristics of Agaru.
AS-2.11.31.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 31 (AS-2.11.31)

AS-2.11.32.text: Asókagrámika, the product of Asókagráma, is of the colour of meat and smells like a lotus flower; Jongaka is reddish yellow and smells like a blue lotus flower or like the urine of a cow; Grameruka is greasy and smells like a cow's urine; Sauvarnakudyaka, product of the country of Suvarnakudya, is reddish yellow and smells like Mátulunga (the fruit of citron tree or sweet lime); Púrnadvipaka, the product of the island, Púrnadviipa, smells like a lotus flower or like butter; Bhadrasríya and Páralauhityaka are of the colour of nutmeg; Antarvatya is of the colour of cascus,---the last two smell like Kushtha (Costus Speciosus); Kaleyaka which is a product of Svarna-bhúmi, gold-producing land, is yellow and greasy; and Auttaraparvataka (a product of, the north mountain) is reddish yellow.
AS-2.11.32.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 32 (AS-2.11.32)

AS-2.11.33.text: The above (fragrant substances) are commodities of superior value (Sára).
AS-2.11.33.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 33 (AS-2.11.33)

AS-2.11.34.text: The smell of the Tailaparnika substances is lasting, no matter whether they are made into a paste or boiled or burnt; also it is neither changed nor affected even when mixed with other substances; and these substances resemble sandal and Agallochum in their qualities.
AS-2.11.34.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 34 (AS-2.11.34)

AS-2.11.35.text: Kántanávaka, Praiyaka, and Auttara-parvataka are the varieties of skins.
AS-2.11.35.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 35 (AS-2.11.35)

AS-2.11.36.text: Kántanávaka is of the colour of the neck of the peacock; Praiyaka is variegated with blue, yellow, and white spots; these two are eight angulas (inches) long.
AS-2.11.36.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 36 (AS-2.11.36)

AS-2.11.37.text: Also Bisí and Mahábisí are the products of Dvádasagráma, twelve villages.
AS-2.11.37.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 37 (AS-2.11.37)

AS-2.11.38.text: That which is of indistinct colour, hairy, and variegated (with spots) is (called) Bisí.
AS-2.11.38.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 38 (AS-2.11.38)

AS-2.11.39.text: That which is rough and almost white is Mahábisí (great Bisí); These two are twelve angulas long.
AS-2.11.39.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 39 (AS-2.11.39)

AS-2.11.4.text: That which is like masúra (ervum hirsutam), that which consists of three joints (triputaka), that which is like a tortoise (kúrmaka), that which is semi-circular, that which consists of several coatings, that which is double (yámaka), that which is scratched, that which is of rough surface, that which is possessed of spots (siktakam), that which is like the water-pot used by an ascetic, that which is of dark-brown or blue colour, and that which is badly perforated are inauspicious.
AS-2.11.4.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 4 (AS-2.11.4)

AS-2.11.40.text: Syámika, Kálika, Kadali, Chandrottara, and Sákulá are (other kinds of skins) procured from Aroha (Arohaja).
AS-2.11.40.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 40 (AS-2.11.40)

AS-2.11.41.text: Syámika is brown and contains variegated spots; Kálika is brown or of the colour of a pigeon; these two are eight angulas long. Kadali is rough and two feet long; when Kadali bears variegated moonlike spots, it is called Chandrottarakadali and is one-third of its length; Sákulá is variegated with large round spots similar to those that manifest themselves in a kind of leprosy (kushtha), or is furnished with tendrils and spotted like a deer's skin.
AS-2.11.41.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 41 (AS-2.11.41)

AS-2.11.42.text: Sámúra, Chínasi, and Sámúli are (skins procured from Báhlava, (Bahlaveya).
AS-2.11.42.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 42 (AS-2.11.42)

AS-2.11.43.text: Sámúra is thirty-six angulas long and black; Chínasi is reddish black or blackish white; Sámúli is of the colour of wheat.
AS-2.11.43.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 43 (AS-2.11.43)

AS-2.11.44.text: Sátina, Nalatúla, and Vrittapuchchha are the skins of aquatic animals (Audra).
AS-2.11.44.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 44 (AS-2.11.44)

AS-2.11.45.text: Sátina is black; Nalatúla is of the colour of the fibre of Nala, a kind of grass; and Vrittapuchchha (that which possesses a round tail) is brown.
AS-2.11.45.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 45 (AS-2.11.45)

AS-2.11.46.text: Blankets made of sheep's wool may be white, purely red, or as red as a lotus flower. They may be made of worsted threads by sewing (khachita); or may be woven of woollen threads of various colour (vánachitra); or may be made of different pieces (khandasanghátya); or may be woven of uniform woollen threads (tantuvichchhinna).
AS-2.11.46.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 46 (AS-2.11.46)

AS-2.11.47.text: Woollen blankets are (of ten kinds):—Kambala, Kauchapaka, Kulamitika, Saumitika, Turagastarana, Varnaka, Talichchhaka, Váravána, Paristoma, and Samantabhadraka.
AS-2.11.47.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 47 (AS-2.11.47)

AS-2.11.48.text: Of these, that which is slippery (pichchhila) as a wet surface, possessed of fine hair, and soft, is the best.
AS-2.11.48.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 48 (AS-2.11.48)

AS-2.11.49.text: That (blanket) which is made up of eight pieces and black in colour is called Bhingisi used as rain-proof ; likewise is Apasáraka; both are the products of Nepal.
AS-2.11.49.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 49 (AS-2.11.49)

AS-2.11.5.text: That which is big, circular, without bottom (nistalam), brilliant, white, heavy, soft to the touch, and properly perforated is the best.
AS-2.11.5.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 5 (AS-2.11.5)

AS-2.11.50.text: Samputika, Chaturasrika, Lambara, Katavánaka, Praváraka, and Sattalika are (blankets made of) the wool of wild animals.
AS-2.11.50.label: Arthashastra Book 2, Chapter 11, Sutra 50 (AS-2.11.50)
